profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a developer tools company after an internal evaluation dashboard showed a sudden drop in the virtual assistant's speech-act classifier performance on bug-repair conversations. The team had just merged a new export pipeline for the Wizard-of-Oz conversation corpus and retrained the model used in an experimental assistant for software engineers. Priya and Ethan are meeting to diagnose why the latest run reports much lower recall than the previous benchmark, even though both believe they are using 'the same dataset' and 'the same evaluation setup.' The agenda is to compare what changed in the data and evaluation flow, identify the most plausible root cause of the regression, and agree on an immediate corrective action for the next training run. The expected outcome is a concrete troubleshooting plan for rerunning the pipeline and a shared decision on what will count as the issue being fixed.

members.name: Priya Nair
members.expertise: NLP model training, dataset versioning, evaluation pipelines for intent and dialogue-act classification
members.background: Priya built the supervised training pipeline for the speech-act detector and recently migrated the corpus preprocessing from notebook-based scripts to a scheduled feature-generation job tied to the internal data lake.
members.private_state: Priya wants to show that the model code is stable and suspects the regression comes from the new corpus export or labeling transformation, but she does not want to openly blame the data team because the migration was partly her proposal.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the bug-repair dataset,' they mean the deduplicated utterance-level training table produced by the new export job, not the raw conversation transcripts.
A 'same split' comparison naturally means preserving the same train/dev/test utterance IDs as the prior benchmark, even if the underlying conversations were re-exported.
If the model is 'back to baseline,' that means macro-averaged precision and recall on the 26-class held-out test split are within normal variance of the previous report.
Rebuilding features from the current data lake snapshot is harmless because the annotations are already finalized and conversation ordering does not materially affect labels.

members.name: Ethan Cole
members.expertise: Empirical software engineering, annotation studies, conversational analysis, experimental validity
members.background: Ethan helped design the Wizard-of-Oz study and the open-coding scheme for the 26 speech act types, and he maintains the benchmark documentation used in research reports and demos.
members.private_state: Ethan wants to preserve comparability with the original paper-style benchmark and is worried the latest run may have drifted away from the evaluation protocol, but he assumes Priya's pipeline still mirrors the documented setup unless stated otherwise.
hidden_assumptions: When people say 'the bug-repair dataset,' they mean the original 30 conversation transcripts with turn order intact, because the speech acts are grounded in conversational context.
A 'same split' comparison means the same conversation-level partition used in the benchmark documentation, not the same utterance rows after reprocessing.

If the model is 'back to baseline,' that means reproducing the headline benchmark trend reported to stakeholders, primarily the earlier precision/recall numbers under the original experimental protocol.
The annotation set is stable, so any export labeled 'v3 finalized' should preserve the original coding decisions and only change formatting, not unit boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the same dataset
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both refer to rerunning on 'the same dataset' or 'the bug-repair dataset.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means the current utterance-level table in the data lake derived from the 30 conversations, after deduplication, assistant-message normalization, and export-time segmentation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan means the original 30 conversation transcripts and annotations as collected in the Wizard-of-Oz study, preserving turn sequence and transcript boundaries.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both know they are talking about the same study corpus and use the familiar project shorthand, so 'same dataset' feels specific enough; neither expects that the other is using a different unit of analysis beneath the same label.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to compare against 'the same split as last time.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya is referring to the stored train/dev/test lists of utterance IDs from the last successful model run after preprocessing.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan is referring to the benchmark's conversation-level split across the 30 two-hour sessions documented for the study.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both have a concrete prior split in mind and each assumes there is only one canonical split worth referencing, so the phrase 'same split' sounds unambiguous in context.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to fix the regression
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the pipeline should be 'back to baseline' before the next demo.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya means the retrained classifier should return to roughly the previous macro test metrics from the internal dashboard, even if the export process or segmentation differs from the historical benchmark.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan means the numbers should once again be comparable to the original benchmark protocol used in the research summary, so that stakeholders can interpret the regression as resolved.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see baseline restoration as an obviously shared goal, and because neither expects disagreement over what a baseline is, they do not spell out whether the criterion is metric recovery or methodological comparability.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to 'rerun preprocessing' before retraining.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Priya plans to rerun the automated feature-generation job on the latest data lake snapshot, which will regenerate segmented utterances and label mappings from current export rules.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Ethan assumes they will rerun only the historical cleaning script over the archived finalized transcripts, preserving the original utterance boundaries and coding structure.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Rerunning preprocessing sounds like a routine maintenance step, and both assume the standard pipeline is already shared knowledge; the hidden divergence lies in which preprocessing path each treats as the default.

When I say the bug-repair dataset, I mean the deduplicated utterance-level table coming out of the new job, because that's what the model actually trains on now.
